(p-275) Surah 107, also called *al-Din*, *Ara'ayta*, *al-Takdhib*, and *al-Ma'un*.

Its purpose is to alert the reader that denying the Resurrection for the sake of the Recompense is the source of all evil (*abu al-khaba'ith*). The one who denies it is repaid with the worst of character traits and the most reprehensible deeds, until belittling the great things (of religion) becomes his disposition, and he becomes one of those who have no portion (*khalaq*). Each of its four names is extremely clear in indicating this, when one reflects on the surah and understands the things it mentions. It forbids reprehensible acts by its explicit statements and calls to noble qualities by its implications and allusions.

﴿In the name of God﴾, whose greatness is exalted above every trace of deficiency, so that He alone possesses all perfection. ﴿The Most Merciful﴾, whose blessing is general, encompassing the good-doer and the wrongdoer, overwhelming all with bounty. ﴿The Most Compassionate﴾, who specially favors His friends by completing His blessing, granting them the delight of union.

* *

When God, glorified and exalted, informed (the reader) of His action toward them, namely the retribution against those who transgressed His limits against them, and of His kindness to them in a way that is the utmost of wisdom, He made it known that the one who does this does not leave people neglected without recompense. He also commanded the last of the Quraysh to thank Him for His blessing by devoting worship to Him alone. At the beginning of this surah, He made known that this cannot be accomplished except by affirming (p-276) the Recompense, which motivates noble character and restrains from its vile forms. He marveled at the one who denies the Recompense despite the clarity of the evidence for it in the wisdom of the All-Wise. He described the denier with attributes from which they (the audience) are most averse, and portrayed him in the most hideous image, to urge them to affirm and to deter them from denial. He addressed specifically the head of the community (the Prophet), as an indication that no one else understands this matter rightly. He said: ﴿Have you seen?﴾, that is, tell me, O most perfect of creation, ﴿the one who denies﴾, that is, who puts denial into effect toward whoever informs him, whoever he may be, ﴿the Recompense﴾, that is, the judgment that takes place on the Day of Resurrection, which is the locus of wisdom and the ultimate aim of the obligatory religion that commands noble character and forbids its evils. Whoever denies one of the two denies the other. Since the verb "to see" here means "to inform me," which takes two objects, the second object is to be understood as: "Is he not deserving of retribution?"

Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When the preceding surahs included threats for those who harbor what is mentioned in them, which proceed from the judgment of ignorance and injustice that are innate in human nature, they included such statements as: ﴿Indeed, man is ungrateful to his Lord﴾ (al-'Adiyat 6), ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ (al-'Asr 2), and ﴿He thinks his wealth will make him immortal﴾ (al-Humazah 3). In the course of this, there arose from these primary attributes other things mentioned in them as well, such as preoccupation with accumulation (al-takathur), slandering and defaming people, and the destructive arrogance of the people of the Elephant. He followed this with mention of attributes that may exist among those who claim to be Muslims, or some of them may exist, or the deeds of those who are characterized by them even if they are not among its people, such as repulsing the orphan, which is pushing him away from his right and not treating him gently, not urging the feeding of the poor, neglecting the prayer and being heedless of it, showing off in deeds, withholding zakat, and withholding the needs that people depend upon one another for. It is possible that the ambiguity of *al-ma'un* includes all of this. There is no doubt that these attributes exist among those who profess Islam. God, glorified and exalted, informed (us) that these are among the attributes of the one who denies the Day of Recompense and does not expect reward or reckoning; that is, these are its people. Of this kind is his statement, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever has four (traits) in him is a pure hypocrite." And his statement, peace and blessings be upon him: "The adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer." This topic is abundant in the Book and the Sunnah, and I have expounded it in my book *Iḍāḥ al-Sabīl min Ḥadīth Su'āl Jibrīl* (Clarifying the Path from the Hadith of Gabriel's Questions). So, of this kind, in my view, and God knows best, is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you seen the one who denies the Recompense?﴾ ﴿That is the one who repulses the orphan﴾ (al-Ma'un 2). That is, these attributes of repulsing the orphan, lacking compassion for him, not urging his feeding, neglecting the prayer, showing off in deeds, and withholding needs (are indicative of this denial), (p-278) for all of these are the nature of one who denies the reckoning and the recompense, because the benefit of abstaining from them only occurs in that state. Whoever affirms it proceeds in these qualities upon the commendable way and the righteous striving, while whoever denies it pays them no heed and disregards all of them. So, O believers, keep yourselves far from them, for they are not among your attributes in the foundation of your faith to which you pledged allegiance. Whoever imitates a people is one of them. Beware of these vices, for repulsing the orphan comes from the arrogance that destroyed the people of the Elephant, and not urging his feeding is the act of the miser who thinks his wealth will make him immortal. Heedlessness toward the prayers is one of the fruits of being distracted by accumulation and preoccupied with wealth and children. Thus He forbade His servants these vile traits, which are produced by what has preceded, and the surahs are joined together. End.

Since the intended meaning of this category is general, and some of the deniers conceal their denial, He described them by signs that arise from the pillar of disbelief from which it springs and branches out. These signs expose them and reveal them, even if they strive to hide it and to appear otherwise. So He said, stating as a consequence of denial what indicates it: ﴿Then that is﴾, that is, the hateful one, far from all good, ﴿who repulses﴾, that is, who pushes away violently with the utmost harshness, ﴿the orphan﴾, and wrongs him, and does not urge the honoring of him, because Allah the Exalted has removed mercy from his heart. He removes it only from a wretch, since nothing moves a person to kindness toward the orphan except fear of Allah, glorified and exalted. Thus denial of its recompense was a cause of harshness toward him [-].

Since the love of the weak is a sign of goodness, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, I ask You for the doing of good deeds, the leaving of evil deeds, and the love of the poor." Harshness toward them is therefore a sign of evil. Whoever is stingy with gentleness in speech is even stingier in giving away his wealth. He [Allah] said, describing [the disbeliever] so that the one who denies the Reckoning is known: his denial brings him down to the lowest of the ranks, and [he has] the worst of qualities, which drives him to the worst of actions: ﴿And does not urge﴾, that is, does not urge himself, his family, or anyone else, with a great urging that would stir him to the desired end, ﴿the feeding of the needy﴾, that is, giving to him and feeding him. Rather, he despises him, does not honor him, and does not show him mercy. The expression of feeding, which is the intended meaning, is given as "food," which is the root, and the attribution of "the needy" [to food] indicates that he [the needy] shares in the wealth of the rich to the extent of the provision that Allah has made obligatory for him. This implies that a sign of denying [the Resurrection] [is] harming the weak and neglecting what is right. The verse is an example of *ihtibak* (a rhetorical device in which one term is left implicit and understood from its counterpart): the rejecting (*da'ʿ*) in the first clause indicates the hatred in (p-280) the second, and the urging (*ḥaḍḍ*) in the second clause indicates its equivalent in the first.

When this was his state toward created beings, He followed it with his state toward the Creator, to inform that each of the two indicates the ruin of the heart and necessitates the abhorrence of the Lord, and the greatest humiliation and distress, and that sins are a destructive ruin, as a warning against them and a caution [against them]. So He made a consequence of it His saying, expressing it with what most indicates humiliation: ﴿Woe﴾. Since the original would have been "for him" with the pronoun and singular, and the intended meaning of "the one who" is the category that applies to one and to more than one.

And whoever belittles the weak because of their weakness turns away from what he does not see and does not perceive because of its absence. Whoever neglects the salah (prayer, the ritual worship) is even more neglectful of what is other than it. Whoever attends to it may think himself saved, even if his attending to it is for the sake of riya' (showing off) or other matters surrounding the act. He expressed it with the attribute, for generality and for attaching the ruling to it, and He qualified it by [the phrase] "of the salah" as a warning against delusion, and as an indication that what produced that baseness in him is what preceded of following a base disposition. He used the plural form as an alert that multiplicity has no honor in His sight, because humiliating a group necessitates humiliating the individuals, without the converse. So He said: ﴿to those who pray﴾.

When the ruling applies to the very place itself, without regard to its description as an act, one knows that what is intended is [the one who is] obligated (*mukallaf*) to perform the prayer, because whoever is engaged in it, like his (ﷺ) saying, "Allah does not accept the prayer of a menstruating woman unless she wears a khimar (head covering)." Therefore He described them by His saying: ﴿who are﴾, that is, in their inner selves and the purity of their hearts. Since the intended meaning is their neglect, He said ﴿of﴾ rather than ﴿in﴾ regarding ﴿their prayer﴾, meaning: it is fitting that it be attributed to them, because it is obligatory upon them and enjoined for their benefit and advantage through purification and other things. ﴿Heedless﴾, that is, deeply immersed in forgetfulness of it, neglecting it, being indifferent to it, and paying it little attention. What clarifies this is that Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) read "*lahun*" (negligent). The benefit of expressing it with a descriptive attribute is to indicate that it is firmly established in them, to such an extent that they do not remember it at all from their own selves; therefore, what follows it explains it. Al-Baghawi narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the verse and said: "It is the wasting of time." And from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: They are the hypocrites who leave the prayer when they are absent, and perform it when they are present with the people.

[p. 281]

Since one who has this characteristic has no regard for anything other than what is present, like the beasts, He said, indicating that what is meant by "heedlessness" here is neglecting the prayer when they are alone in abandoning it, both outwardly and inwardly, and when they are in company, by corrupting it in meaning: ﴿Those who﴾, that is, with all of their inner selves, ﴿make show﴾, that is, with their prayer and other deeds, they show people that they are doing good so that people will see them, and thereby they receive praise from them and kindness toward them, even if only by holding back from them what they deserve of the sword, not seeking reward nor fearing the punishment of Allah, glorified and exalted be He. For this reason they abandon the prayer when they are away from people.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 107, verse 7:

When someone who has this attribute sometimes does a little good but not much of it, out of showing off, He made clear that stinginess had overcome them so thoroughly that, even with their abundant showing off, they could not bring themselves to show off with this trivial thing. They stripped themselves of all the qualities of generosity. So, to intensify their condemnation and to indicate that the most beloved of creatures to God is the one who is most beneficial to his dependents, He said: ﴿and they withhold﴾, meaning continually, over time. The first object is omitted to generalize, so that it includes everyone, however great or high-ranking they are and however dear they are to the hearts of these people. This makes clear that they had reached such baseness that there is no further level in which envy could find a place. ﴿al-Ma'un﴾ (small household necessities) means the rights of property and the small benefits, such as lending trivial household goods, which people customarily lend to one another. They also withhold from the needy what God has made obligatory for them in their wealth of rights. The upshot is that this should be understood as the withholding of what must be given, such as surplus pasture and water, the zakat (obligatory alms), and the like, so that it would bring about the threat of woe. 'Ali, Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, al-Hasan, and Qatada interpreted it as zakat. The scholars said: it is derived from *al-ma'n* (a small amount), (p. 283) which in the language means a small thing. For this reason some interpreted it as water, some as household goods lent out, such as a cooking pot, an axe, and a bucket, and some as zakat, because only a very small amount is taken from property as zakat relative to the whole. It was also said that it is every gift or benefit. Qutrub said: it is *fa'ul* from *al-ma'n*, and *al-ma'n* means kindness. Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-ma'un* in the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic period) meant giving and benefit, and in Islam it meant zakat. Al-Harawi said: Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: it is the loan of goods. This was mentioned by the teacher 'Abd al-Haqq al-Ishbili in his book *al-Wa'i*. Ibn Jarir said: the root of *al-ma'un* is the benefit of anything.

This indicates that they reached the extreme of denial, by treating with contempt the greatest pillars of the religion and by magnifying the smallest worldly matters. This last meaning, as you see, is the first, because what leads to it is denial. Whoever withholds these trivial things is more deserving of being prevented from receiving al-Kawthar (the river in Paradise) on the Day of Gathering. Just as the last part of the surah meets the first, the whole surah meets its counterpart in number from the beginning of the Qur'an. That is because he knows that the essential purpose of this surah is to keep away from the base and low qualities of character, from denial (p. 284) of the recompense, which is the wisdom of existence, and which produces turning away from fulfilling the rights of creatures and obeying the Creator, and from being drawn, together with deficiencies, to contempt for the weak, which only the basest and most degraded of people show, and to showing off, which only one who is in the extreme of lowness commits. Therefore this leads to an inclination toward the greatest woe. In this there is the strongest encouragement toward the noble qualities of character, which are the opposites of what is mentioned in the surah. Both matters are present in al-Anfal, which corresponds to it in returning the ending to the beginning, in the most complete manner, so that this would be an indication that it explains this surah. Thus there is an allusion to considering it when reciting it. Look at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who establish prayer and spend from what We have provided them﴾ (8:3), ﴿It is those who are truly believers﴾ (8:4), the verse ﴿And when they said: O God, if this is indeed the truth from You…﴾ (8:32), ﴿And their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping﴾ (8:35), ﴿Those who disbelieve will be gathered to Hell﴾ (8:36), the verse ﴿And know that for God is one-fifth of it, and for the Messenger and for the near relatives and the orphans and the needy and the traveler﴾ (8:41), the verse ﴿And do not be like those who went out from their homes in insolence and to be seen by people﴾ (8:47). The surah has truly fit, with its meanings, its great structures, its arrangements, and its constructions, upon the lowest, most abject, and basest people. Its words surrounded their heads, individually, before its letters, and it passed around to them the cups of their deaths from the points of spears in the hands of its soldiers and the sharp edges of its swords. (p. 285) This is because the number of its words is twenty-five words. If you count them from the first years of the prophethood, they correspond to the twelfth year of the Hijra (migration), which was the last part of the caliphate of al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him. In that year, none remained at his hand of those who prayed and who apostatized from Islam after the death of the Prophet ﷺ or who withheld zakat. It became clear that they had not prayed or paid zakat during his lifetime ﷺ except to be seen by people, like the base and impure. Woe befell them at the hands of the soldiers of al-Siddiq, who came to them on foot and on horseback and tore them apart completely. That year had not passed before he had finished with them by finishing with the Banu Hanifa at al-Yamama and the outlying regions of Yemen, including the people of al-Najir in the lands of Kinda, and al-Aswad al-'Ansi in San'a. The year sixteen, which corresponds to the number of words with the basmala, passed, and that was at the beginning of the caliphate of al-Faruq. Until they were removed from the whole Arabian Peninsula, both the polytheist Arabs, their Christianized ones, and their Zoroastrianized ones who were in the regions of Iraq, Syria, and Bahrain. Most of them became Muslims, and the rest went to the lands of the Romans. Thus woe befell the hypocrites among the people of prayer, for they were the ones to whom their Prophet ﷺ came with prayer, and they turned away from it, while people followed them. It is not valid in this surah to consider the pronouns, because the religion had reached, at this limit, to have prevailed over every apparent thing, to a point where there is no concealment in it in any way, no obstacle to it, and no veil. Just as there is no need for symbolic reference through pronouns, because of the glad tidings that reached the two horizons, upon the tops of the pulpits and minarets, so too it is not fitting, after arriving at this manifest state, to allude by indicating through the arrangement of the letters. And God knows best what is correct, and to Him is the return and the final destination.
